opus-5.5.text:
I think interpretability is one goal, but it's not the only one, and I want to be careful about how we frame it.

When people say "interpretability," they often mean something very engineering-oriented: you have a big model, you open it up, and you try to find which neuron or which circuit is responsible for some behavior. That's valuable, but from a physics perspective I see it a bit differently. In physics, we don't just want to explain one particular system. We want to find general principles, laws that hold across many systems. So for me, Physics of AI is about understanding *why* neural networks behave the way they do, and interpretability is one window into that.

Here's an analogy I like. Before thermodynamics, people built steam engines. They worked, but nobody really knew why. Then thermodynamics and statistical mechanics came along and gave us concepts like temperature, entropy, and phase transitions. Those concepts didn't require tracking every molecule. They were the right level of description. I think AI is in a similar stage. We have very powerful engines, but we're still searching for the right concepts and the right level of abstraction.

So interpretability, in my view, means finding those good abstractions. Sometimes that's microscopic: looking at representations and seeing, for example, that a network has learned a circle structure to do modular arithmetic. That was one thing we saw in our work on grokking. The representation suddenly becomes structured, and that structure explains the generalization. Sometimes it's more macroscopic: understanding training dynamics, scaling behavior, or phase transitions between memorization and generalization, without needing to know every weight.

I also think interpretability should be pursued not only after the fact but by design. That's part of the motivation behind things like Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks. Instead of training a black box and then trying to pry it open, can we build models whose structure is closer to how scientists think, so the learned function can be read, simplified, and maybe even turned into a symbolic formula? For scientific applications especially, that's very important, because the goal isn't only prediction. It's understanding.

And finally, there's a practical side. If we really understand the mechanisms, we can make models more efficient, more reliable, and safer. Physics didn't just satisfy curiosity. It let us engineer things much better. I hope Physics of AI can do the same: interpretability gives us understanding, and understanding eventually gives us better control and better design.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts neuron- or circuit-level analysis with broader abstractions and says macroscopic understanding need not account for every weight.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention changing random seeds or explain that this could invalidate an account of internal mechanisms.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I talk about interpretability within Physics of AI, I don't mean it the way it's often used in the mechanistic interpretability community, where the goal is to open up a specific trained network and reverse-engineer every circuit. That work is valuable, but it's closer to anatomy or neuroscience. What I have in mind is something more like what physics did for the natural world.

Physics never understood nature by tracking every atom. It found a small number of concepts and laws, like energy, entropy, phase transitions, that explain a huge range of phenomena at the right level of abstraction. So when I say interpretability is a goal of Physics of AI, I mean: can we find the analogous concepts for neural networks? Can we explain why a model learns what it learns, why scaling laws look the way they do, why grokking happens, why certain architectures generalize and others don't, in terms of a few principles rather than a pile of empirical observations?

There's a tension here that I find really interesting. Physics has traditionally studied systems that we didn't design, and the laws were there to be discovered. Neural networks are things we built, and yet we don't understand them. That's almost embarrassing, but it's also an opportunity, because we have complete access. We can measure everything, run controlled experiments, build toy models that isolate one phenomenon at a time. That's exactly the physicist's methodology: simplify until you can understand, then check whether the understanding survives when you add the complexity back.

I also think interpretability goes in two directions. One direction is understanding existing models after the fact. The other, which I care about a lot, is designing models to be interpretable from the start. My work on Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks came partly from that motivation. If you can make the building blocks transparent, so that a trained model can be read off as a formula or a structure a scientist recognizes, then interpretability isn't something you bolt on afterward, it's baked in. And then AI becomes a genuine collaborator in science, not just a black-box oracle.

So in short: interpretability, to me, means reaching the level of understanding where we could have predicted the behavior before running the experiment. That's the standard physics holds itself to, and I think AI should aspire to the same.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Physics of AI with reverse-engineering every circuit in a specific network and describes explaining behavior through higher-level principles.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention random seeds or say that changing a seed can invalidate an explanation of internal mechanisms.

astra-6.text:
I think interpretability, from the perspective of physics of AI, means finding simple principles behind a very complicated system. A neural network has so many parameters that even if you can inspect every one of them, that doesn’t necessarily mean you understand how it works.

In physics, we face this situation all the time. A gas contains an enormous number of molecules, but we can describe its behavior using quantities like temperature and pressure. So for AI, we can ask: What are the right quantities to measure? What kinds of structure emerge during learning? Can we find a simple model that explains those structures and predicts when they will change?

Understanding individual neurons or circuits can be useful, but I wouldn’t make that the only goal. We also want an explanation at the level where the behavior becomes simple. And ideally, that explanation should let us make predictions—if we change the data, the architecture, or the training process, what will happen? To me, that predictive power is an important test of whether we really understand the system.

r001.rationale: The response says understanding individual neurons or circuits can be useful but should not be the only goal, and emphasizes explanations at a level where behavior becomes simple.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention random seeds or say that changing a seed can invalidate an explanation of internal mechanisms.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of interpretability as turning the behavior of an AI system into something we can understand scientifically. In physics, we don’t just predict what a system will do; we try to identify the relevant variables, discover relationships between them, and explain why those relationships emerge. I would like us to have that kind of understanding of neural networks.

There are different levels of understanding. You might ask what a particular neuron represents, how a circuit performs a computation, or why a model develops a certain capability during training. Those questions are related, but an explanation at one level doesn’t automatically answer the others.

For me, the goal is to find simple explanations that are also testable. If we think a model uses a particular mechanism, can we intervene on it and predict how the model’s behavior will change? Can that understanding transfer across models or training conditions? That’s where interpretability becomes more than an appealing story—it becomes a way to build and test a scientific theory of AI.

r001.rationale: The response lists neuron-level questions alongside other levels, but does not say interpretability need not reach neuron-level explanations.
